messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam, a 56-year-old detective of Oceania background, came to treatment after years of carrying a childhood that still seemed to sit inside every shift and every quiet moment at home. He described being raised by a caregiver whose physical abuse was sudden, humiliating, and impossible to predict: the smell of something burnt in the kitchen would sometimes be the only warning before a blow, and even now that same acrid scent could pull him back without preparation to the cramped rooms, the heat, and the fear of waiting for what came next. He had learned to scan people quickly, especially those who looked like the men who had hurt him in childhood, and to mistrust even small flashes of warmth or ease. The smell did not just remind him of the abuse; it would drag him straight back into one of those childhood rooms, so vividly that for a moment he was no longer in the present at all. A burnt pan at home or scorched wiring at the station could do it before he had time to steady himself. When that burnt smell came up at work or on the street, Liam would stop what he was doing, move away from people, and keep checking the room until he felt he had some control again; the reminder itself drove the avoidance and the constant watchfulness. It was easier to add distance than to risk being caught off guard by it again. What unsettled him most was that positive emotion itself could feel dangerous, as if a rare moment of relief was the moment before something terrible happened. When he tried to talk about what had happened, he often lost the thread entirely and could not finish the story, and he would come away feeling that his own reactions proved he was a lousy coper and that there must be something fundamentally wrong with the kind of person he was. The more he told himself that he should have handled it better, the more the memory seemed to come forward on its own, as if his mind kept returning him to the scene to prove the point he feared was true. His self-blame made the abuse feel less like something that had happened to him and more like evidence that he was weak. Over time, those beliefs had hardened into a conviction that the world did not operate by any rules he could trust; it had, in his words, “completely broken” the way he thought life was supposed to work.

Those meanings fed his memory in painful ways. When Liam tried to explain the abuse, the account would fragment, and the more he struggled to tell it in order, the more his mind would snap to vivid, uninvited scenes: a hand raised, the stale heat of the room, the burnt smell hanging in the air. The recollection was not distant or narrative in shape; it arrived with the force of something happening again, and with it came intense rage that made his jaw clench and his chest tighten. He said that the memory could be triggered instantly by something in his surroundings, as though his mind had learned to stand ready for a return of the old danger. Once it had burst back like that, he started noticing possible warnings everywhere — the whine of wiring, the smell of a kitchen gone too hot, the hard set of a stranger’s face. After the memory had flooded him, ordinary details began to look like they might be the next sign of trouble. At work, in the station or out on a scene, if he caught even a faint burnt odor from wiring, a kitchen fire, or scorched material, he would be thrown back into the abuse before he had time to think. If someone in the street or in a file photo resembled one of the victims he had seen over the years, he would feel the memory sharpen again, not only of the childhood assaults but of his own powerlessness in the face of them. Feeling that danger so constantly made his view of himself harsher, and he came to take it as proof that his life had been altered in some permanent way. The threat he felt every day quietly confirmed his belief that he was not the kind of man who got to feel safe. His belief that his world had been shattered, and that he himself had somehow invited the treatment, kept the memories bound to shame and anger rather than history. The more he blamed himself, the more the scenes seemed to confirm that he had been weak all along, and the more he tried to explain, the less coherent the story became.

To manage this, Liam narrowed his life. He avoided other people whenever he could, ate lunch alone, and found reasons not to linger after work. He had even started avoiding clothes that resembled what he had worn at certain times in childhood, because the wrong shirt could make him feel exposed and stranded in an old role he hated. The more he kept the experience at a distance, the less it seemed to stay put; weeks of not talking about it left the memory intact and raw, so that when it did surface it came back with a force that felt fresh. What he had thought would keep him safe had, in practice, kept the scene close to hand. At the same time, pulling away from people and from the memories gave the recollections more room to intrude. When he detached himself from them, they returned less as something observed than as something that broke through abruptly, and that unpredictability made him even more alert. Each time he chose to leave early, sit apart, or keep his distance, the decision carried its own quiet message: that he needed those precautions because he could not simply cope like other people. Over time, those habits became another source of the belief that he was fragile and permanently behind everyone else. He remained superalert at home and on duty, having difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay watchful, and he noticed that his body reacted strongly whenever something reminded him of the abuse. He would jolt at small sounds, pace the house, and keep checking the door or the stove, as though the next threat might be waiting in the ordinary details of the room. That constant guardedness made it easier for the burnt smell, the sight of a similar face, or even a burst of unexpected happiness to catch him unprepared, and each fresh reminder seemed to confirm his conviction that the world could turn instantly. The more he withdrew and monitored for danger, the more isolated and self-critical he became, certain that these were the failures of a man who had not coped well enough and who could never quite keep himself safe.

By the time he sought help, the cycle had begun to cost him his marriage, his sleep, and his confidence at work. He was still functioning as a detective, but he was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard and frightened that one wrong smell or one unexpected moment of feeling good would throw him back into the old scenes in front of colleagues or suspects. What brought him in was the sense that the life he had built around vigilance was shrinking, and that he was becoming more cut off from everyone he cared about. He said he wanted relief, but what he feared most was that the memories would keep arriving without warning and prove, once again, that he was not someone who could ever truly withstand them.
